t: The Ājīvikas taught niyati, absolute determinism: everything that has happened, is happening and will happen is preordained by cosmic principles, there is no free will, and the karma doctrine is a fallacy.
Their own scriptures are lost, so everything known of them comes from Buddhist, Jain and other texts, written largely by rivals, and scholars question how fairly these describe them.

Ashoka's inscriptions in the Barabar Caves in Bihar, the oldest surviving cave temples of ancient India, record his gifts to the Ājīvikas; tax inscriptions show the school in southern India until 1346.
dyk: In several Barabar Cave inscriptions the word “Ājīvikas” was later chiselled out, probably by religious rivals while the Brahmi script was still understood; the original lettering is so deep that it can still be read.
ev: Makkhali Gosala, generally considered the founder of the Ājīvikas, lives as a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira
Ashoka dedicates Barabar Caves to the Ājīvikas in the 12th year of his reign; further dedications follow in his 19th year, about 251 BCE
After the decline of the Maurya Empire the Ājīvikas find only occasional mention in Sanskrit literature
The Pallava king Simhavarman II is the earliest ruler of a series of southern Indian inscriptions that record a tax on Ājīvikas
Varahamihira's Brhaj-jataka mentions the Ājīvikas among the major ascetic groups
The Jain commentator Mallisena, writing the Syadvada-manjari, suggests that the Ājīvikas still existed in his time
The last dated inscription recording a tax on Ājīvikas or Acuvas is set up near Kolar

f.origin: northern India, generally held to be in the 5th century BCE, though the exact origins are unknown; Buddhist and Jain texts name Savatthi (Śrāvastī) as the hub of the Ājīvikas
f.founder: Makkhali Gosala (Sanskrit Gośala Maskariputra, c. 484 BCE) is generally considered the founder; some sources call him only the leader of a large congregation, and Jarl Charpentier and others suggest the tradition is older
f.scriptures: lost: the primary texts are said to have included the ten Purvas (eight Mahanimittas and two Maggas) and the Onpatu Katir, but the movement is known only from the writings of Buddhists, Jains and others
f.followers: none: the last dated inscription that mentions a tax on Ājīvikas is of 1346 CE, and stray references to survivors run to the 15th century
